nations.lands: Old Crow and the surrounding homeland in northern Yukon, Canada

facts.text: Old Crow, a fly-in community of about 300 people on the Porcupine River, is the seat of the Vuntut Gwitchin government.
Dinjii Zhuh k'yuu, the Gwich'in language, is the official language of the Vuntut Gwitchin First Nation, which is training teachers and raising young speakers.

nations.name: Imazighen
nations.lands: North Africa (Tamazgha): Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt's Siwa oasis, with communities across the Sahel and in the diaspora

facts.text: Each 30 August, Amazigh Flag Day marks the flag's adoption in 1997 by Amazigh representatives from across North Africa and the diaspora.

source.title: Jour du drapeau Amazigh
source.publisher: Congrès Mondial Amazigh / Amazigh World Congress

nations.name: Griqua
nations.lands: the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa

facts.text: Griqua communities live today in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: Early Griqua communities governed themselves through leaders called kaptyns, with magistrates drawn from leading families.

nations.name: Oromo
nations.lands: Oromia and other regions of Ethiopia, and northern Kenya

facts.text: Knowledge of the Gada system is passed on to Oromo children today, at home and at school.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo

facts.text: UNESCO lists the Gada system as an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo, inscribed on its heritage list in 2016.

source.title: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo

nations.name: Ishelhiyen
nations.lands: the Souss valley, the Anti-Atlas and the western High Atlas of south-western Morocco

facts.text: In the Souss-Massa region, 63.2% of residents use Tachelhit, the language of the Ishelhin, according to Morocco's 2024 census.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Souss-Massa
source.publisher: Haut-Commissariat au Plan (HCP), Direction Régionale de Souss Massa

facts.text: Tachelhit, the language of the Ishelhin of southern Morocco, is one of three Amazigh languages taught at Inalco in Paris.

source.title: Kabyle (Berber)
source.publisher: Inalco (Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales)

nations.name: Hai//om
nations.lands: north-central Namibia, in and around Etosha National Park and on resettlement farms in Kunene, Oshikoto and Oshana regions

facts.text: Many Hai//om communities lived on lands that are now Etosha National Park and the surrounding regions, according to the Hai//om Community San Council.

source.title: Challenges Faced by the Hai//om San Marginalized Communities in Namibia: Challenges and Solutions
source.publisher: Cultural Survival (by the Hai//om Community San Council)

facts.text: Hai//om heritage includes their own language, storytelling, music and traditional knowledge, and the council calls for mother-tongue teaching in early grades.

source.title: Challenges Faced by the Hai//om San Marginalized Communities in Namibia: Challenges and Solutions
source.publisher: Cultural Survival (by the Hai//om Community San Council)

nations.name: Naro
nations.lands: Ghanzi District in western Botswana, and eastern Namibia

facts.text: Botswana chose Naro, the main San language of Ghanzi District, as one of the mother-tongue languages for primary school teaching from 2022.

source.title: Forty years of fighting for literacy The case of Naro Bible translators

facts.text: Naro's alphabet was created in Botswana through a language project begun in the 1980s, and Naro pioneers wrote songs and other texts in it. The project is based in D'Kar.

source.title: Forty years of fighting for literacy The case of Naro Bible translators

nations.name: Tshwa
nations.lands: Tsholotsho and Bulilimamangwe districts of western Zimbabwe

facts.text: Zimbabwe's 2013 Constitution lists Koisan among its 16 languages, and in 2023 the Tsoro-o-tso San Development Trust worked on the Tjwao language.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Zimbabwe chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: About 3,207 Tshwa live in Zimbabwe, where they self-identify as an Indigenous people, mostly in the western districts.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Zimbabwe chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Endorois
nations.lands: around Lake Bogoria in Baringo County, and in Nakuru and Laikipia counties, in Kenya's Rift Valley

facts.text: The Endorois Welfare Council, founded in 1995 by senior members of the community, works for justice and sustainable development for the Endorois.

source.title: Endorois Welfare Council - Endorois Welfare Council for marginalized communities

nations.name: Yiaku
nations.lands: Mukogodo Forest in Laikipia County, Kenya

facts.text: Yiaku women and elders now lead language teaching and forest care, and growing youth involvement is strengthening the community.

source.title: Reviving Indigenous forest stewardship
source.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)

facts.text: Since 2003 the Yiaku Laikipiak Trust has worked to protect Mukogodo Forest and keep Yiaku culture alive.

source.title: Reviving Indigenous forest stewardship
source.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)

nations.name: Anywaa
nations.lands: Gambella in western Ethiopia, along the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers, and neighbouring South Sudan

facts.text: Anywaa activists helped found EMIPRO in 2022, the first legally registered Indigenous-led rights organization in Ethiopia.

source.title: “We Belong to This Land:” The Anywaa Peoples’ Fight for Survival, Dignity, and Recognition in Ethiopia

facts.text: The Anywaa are river farmers and fishers whose lives follow the Akobo, Alwaro, Openo (Baro) and Gilo rivers of Gambella.

source.title: “We Belong to This Land:” The Anywaa Peoples’ Fight for Survival, Dignity, and Recognition in Ethiopia

nations.name: Toubou
nations.lands: the Tibesti plateau of northern Chad, southern Libya along the Chad border, and northern Niger

facts.text: Toubou herders practise mobile pastoralism across a wide area stretching from northern Niger to Sudan.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Libya chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: About 50,000 Toubou live in Libya along the border with Chad; the people's origins lie in the Tibesti plateau.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Libya chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: Rifians
nations.lands: the Rif of northern and north-eastern Morocco, including Al Hoceima province

facts.text: In Morocco's 2024 census, 53.6% of people in Al Hoceima province said they use Tarifit, the language of the Irifiyen.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima

facts.text: Nationwide, 3.2% of Morocco's population reported Tarifit among the local languages they use, in the 2024 census.

source.title: RGPH 2024: Caractéristiques démographiques et socioéconomiques de la population, Région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima

nations.name: Baka
nations.lands: forests of eastern and southern Cameroon, northern Gabon, and neighbouring parts of the Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic

facts.text: In Gabon, the Baka are one of nine Indigenous forest peoples, alongside the Babongo, Bakoya and others, each with its own language and culture.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Gabon chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: A 2021 agreement signed with the Baka association ASBABUK gives Baka communities around Lobéké National Park access for their traditional activities in the park.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Cameroon chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

nations.name: !Xun
nations.lands: north-eastern Namibia and southern Angola, and Platfontein near Kimberley in South Africa

facts.text: In South Africa, !Xun and Khwe communities live mainly at Platfontein, near Kimberley.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

facts.text: XK FM, a public station first on air in 2000, now broadcasts from Platfontein about 15 hours a day in the !Xun and Khwe languages.

source.title: MEDIA STATEMENT | SABC CELEBRATES THE HISTORY AND CULTURE OF THE !XU AND KHWE

nations.name: Mozabite
nations.lands: the M'Zab valley around Ghardaïa in the Algerian Sahara

facts.text: UNESCO credits the M'Zab with an ingenious system for capturing and sharing water which, with its palm groves, makes life work in a semi-desert.
The M'Zab valley habitat, built in the tenth century by the Ibadites around five ksour (fortified towns), survives intact and is UNESCO World Heritage.

nations.name: BaAka
nations.lands: forests between the Oubangui and Sangha rivers, in south-western Central African Republic and northern Republic of the Congo

facts.text: Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas credits BaAka knowledge of the forest as central to its research, conservation and tourism work.
BaAka singing is four-voice polyphony mastered by the whole community. UNESCO first recognized it in 2003 and inscribed it on its heritage list in 2008.

source.title: Polyphonic singing of the Aka Pygmies of Central Africa

nations.name: Southern Ute Indian Tribe
nations.lands: Southern Ute Reservation around Ignacio, southwestern Colorado, United States

facts.text: The Southern Ute Indian Tribe is made up of the Mouache and Caputa bands and is headquartered in Ignacio, Colorado.
Under a May 11, 2026 agreement with Interior, the Southern Ute Indian Tribe can approve covered energy and mineral leases, agreements and rights-of-way on its reservation trust lands.

source.title: Southern Ute Indian Tribe Celebrates Signing of Tribal Energy Resource Agreement

nations.name: San Carlos Apache
nations.lands: Gila, Graham and Pinal counties, southeastern Arizona, US

facts.text: The San Carlos Apache Reservation, set aside in 1871, covers 1,834,781 acres reaching from alpine meadows to desert in southeastern Arizona.
More than a third of San Carlos land is forest or woodland, giving a home to elk, mule deer, black bear, turkeys and mountain lion.

nations.name: A:shiwi
nations.lands: Pueblo of Zuni along the Zuni River in western New Mexico, US, with reservation land in Arizona

facts.text: The Pueblo of Zuni counts about 18,692 people and holds about 463,287 acres of reservation land.
For about the last 300 years most Zuni people have lived in one main village, the Pueblo of Zuni, with farming villages used at planting and harvest.

nations.name: Lipan Apache Tribe
nations.lands: Texas, United States, with tribal administration in McAllen and historical homelands spanning Texas and northern Mexico

facts.text: The Lipan Apache Tribe in Texas maintains a Tribal Council responsible for community welfare and protection of its heritage.
In 2021, the City and County of Presidio donated a Lipan cemetery parcel to the Lipan Apache Tribe.

source.title: El Cementerio de los Lipanes Transferred to Tribe

nations.name: Ute Indian Tribe
also: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation
nations.lands: Uintah and Ouray Reservation, northeastern Utah, with tribal government at Fort Duchesne, United States

facts.text: In an April 2026 statement, the Ute Indian Tribe announced it would appeal a federal district court decision concerning split-estate reservation lands.

source.title: Tribe will appeal Utah Federal District Court decision on split estate lands

facts.text: The Ute Indian Tribe elects Business Committee representatives from the Uintah, Uncompahgre and Whiteriver bands.

nations.name: Taos Pueblo
nations.lands: Taos valley, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: Tiwa is the native language of Taos Pueblo, and English and Spanish are also spoken there.
In 1970 a federal law returned 48,000 acres, including Blue Lake, to Taos Pueblo, a landmark for tribal self-determination across the United States.

nations.name: Wixárika
nations.lands: Sierra Madre Occidental in Jalisco and Nayarit, Mexico, with communities in Durango and Zacatecas

facts.text: At the end of the 1700s Wixárika communities received land titles that defined the boundaries of their present-day communities.

source.title: Huicholes
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: In July 2025 UNESCO added the Wixárika Route through sacred sites to Wirikuta, a 500 km corridor, to the World Heritage List after decades of Wixaritari requests.

source.title: Boletín No. 334: La Ruta Wixárika por los sitios sagrados a Wirikuta es inscrita en la Lista de Patrimonio Mundial de la UNESCO
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH)

nations.name: Acoma
nations.lands: Acoma Mesa and surrounding lands in west-central New Mexico, US

facts.text: In 1999 Acoma set up a Historic Preservation Office to keep traditional skills alive, among them stone cutting, wood carving, pottery making and weaving.
Archaeologists agree that Acoma has been lived in continuously since at least AD 1200, and Acoma oral history reaches back much further.

nations.name: Southern Paiute
nations.lands: Southern Utah and northern Arizona, US, including Cedar City, Utah, and the Kaibab reservation near Fredonia, Arizona

facts.text: The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Restoration Act of April 3, 1980 brought formal federal recognition to the Cedar Band of Paiute Indians.
The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah shares The Paiute Language for Beginners, now in its second edition, which anyone can view and download.

nations.name: Rarámuri
nations.lands: Sierra Tarahumara in Chihuahua, Mexico, with smaller communities in Durango, Sonora and Sinaloa

facts.text: Rarámuri artisans make violins, drums, palm baskets, clay pots and wooden masks, and sell them in towns such as Guachochi, Creel and Batopilas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: The Rarámuri ball race is a contest in which runners cover long distances while kicking a wooden ball, and it is held as part of community fiestas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Tohono O’odham
nations.lands: Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona, US (Sells is the capital), with O’odham communities across the border in Sonora, Mexico

facts.text: Divided by the border since the 1850s, O’odham communities in Sonora, Mexico, and Arizona still share a common culture and sense of being one people.

source.title: Pápagos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

facts.text: O’odham groups still speak the O’odham language, part of the Uto-Aztecan family, with dialects that vary from group to group.

nations.name: Hopi
nations.lands: Hopitutskwa, northeastern Arizona, US (Navajo and Coconino counties)

facts.text: Hopi government is unicameral. Its powers rest with a Tribal Council of village representatives, who serve two year terms.
The Hopi Reservation in northeastern Arizona covers more than 1.5 million acres and is made up of 12 villages on three mesas.

source.title: The Official Website of the Hopi Tribe

nations.name: Kha’P’o
nations.lands: From the eastern Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande, northern New Mexico, US

facts.text: People of Santa Clara Pueblo still speak the Tewa language today and carry on their customs and cultural activities.
Santa Clara is one of six Tewa-speaking villages, and its reservation covers about 90 square miles from the Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande.

nations.name: Kumeyaay
nations.lands: San Diego and Imperial counties, California, US, and Tecate, Ensenada and Rosarito in Baja California, Mexico

facts.text: North of the US and Mexico border there are 12 Kumeyaay Nation bands today, each original to Kumeyaay territory. Sycuan is one of them.

source.title: History & Heritage
source.publisher: Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation

facts.text: In Baja California the Kumiai call themselves Tipai. Their communities sit on the coastal plateaus of Ensenada and Rosarito and in Tecate.

source.title: Kumiais
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

nations.name: Yoeme
nations.lands: Yaqui River valley in Sonora, Mexico, and Pascua Yaqui communities near Tucson, Arizona, US

facts.text: Most Yoeme people today live in the Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa, and the federally recognized Pascua Yaqui Tribe is based in Tucson, Arizona.
The Pascua Yaqui Tribe in Arizona gained United States federal recognition on September 18, 1978.

nations.name: Chiricahua Apache Nation
nations.lands: Headquarters in Santa Clara, New Mexico, United States; this record describes this named community, not every Chiricahua Apache person or government

facts.text: The Chiricahua Apache Nation lists its tribal headquarters in Santa Clara, New Mexico.
Its foundation's stated work includes education, social welfare and defending Chiricahua Apache self-determination.

nations.name: Shipibo-Konibo
nations.lands: Ucayali, Madre de Dios, Loreto and Huánuco in Peru, with an urban community at Cantagallo in Lima

facts.text: Cantagallo, home to Shipibo-Konibo families, is the best known Amazonian Indigenous settlement in metropolitan Lima.

source.title: Shipibo-Konibo | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Peru's 2017 national census, 25,232 people identified as part of the Shipibo-Konibo people.

source.title: Shipibo-Konibo | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Tupinambá
nations.lands: Atlantic Forest of southern Bahia around Olivença, in Ilhéus, Buerarema and Una, with Tupinambá communities also in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: The Tupinambá of Olivença live in the Atlantic Forest region of southern Bahia.
In 2001 Funai, Brazil's Indigenous affairs agency, officially recognized the Tupinambá of Olivença as an Indigenous people.

nations.name: Guarani Kaiowá
nations.lands: Southern Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, and neighboring eastern Paraguay, where the people are known as Paĩ Tavyterã

facts.text: Kaiowá, Ñandeva and Mbya Guarani all speak dialects of Guarani and show strong energy in keeping their language alive.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

facts.text: Guarani communities today call the places they live tekoha, a word that joins land, forest, fields, water, animals, plants and medicines.

source.title: Guarani Kaiowá - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

nations.name: Mẽbêngôkre
nations.lands: Forests and savannas of southern Pará and northern Mato Grosso, Brazil, along rivers of the Xingu basin such as the Iriri, Bacajá and Fresco

facts.text: The Associação Floresta Protegida, created in 1998 by Mẽbêngôkre leaders, represents about 3,000 people in 31 villages across three Indigenous lands.
The Mẽbêngôkre language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.

nations.name: Yanomami
nations.lands: Forests of Amazonas and Roraima states in northern Brazil, continuing across the border into southern Venezuela

facts.text: The Yanomami Indigenous Territory in Brazil, about 9.66 million hectares of tropical forest, was ratified by presidential decree on 25 May 1992.

nations.name: Awajún
nations.lands: Northern Peruvian Amazon in Amazonas, Loreto, San Martín, Cajamarca and Ucayali

facts.text: The Federation of Aguaruna Women of the Upper Marañón (FEMAAM), founded in Imaza in 2002, opened the way for Awajún women's political participation.

source.title: Awajún | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: The Awajún language belongs to the Jivaroan language family.

source.title: Awajún | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Wichí
nations.lands: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, mainly Salta, Formosa and Chaco provinces, with related communities in southern Bolivia

facts.text: In 2010 Argentina's Chaco province made the Wichí, Qom and Moqoit languages official languages of the province alongside Spanish.

source.title: Argentine: les lois provinciales à portée linguistique
source.publisher: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)

nations.name: Pueblo Originario Kichwa de Sarayaku
nations.lands: Middle Bobonaza river basin, Pastaza province, Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: Sarayaku has its own statute on image, communication and digital sovereignty, setting free, prior and informed consent rules for visitors, press and researchers.

source.title: Statute of Governance of Image, Communication, and Digital Sovereignty of the Kichwa Indigenous People of Sarayaku

facts.text: Sarayaku's Kawsak Sacha (Living Forest) proposal seeks legal recognition of the living forest as a new category of protected land.

nations.name: Qom
nations.lands: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, especially Chaco, Formosa and Santa Fe provinces, plus communities in Buenos Aires and in Paraguay

facts.text: The Qom language is being recovered in universities and in community-run spaces, and children and teenagers are taking it up.

source.title: El wichí y el qom comienzan a ser hablados en la primera infancia y en la adolescencia
source.publisher: Unidiversidad, Universidad Nacional de Cuyo (from Télam)

facts.text: Qom is one of three Indigenous languages that Argentina's Chaco province declared official alongside Spanish in 2010.

source.title: Argentine: les lois provinciales à portée linguistique
source.publisher: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)

nations.name: Munduruku
nations.lands: Tapajós river basin in Pará, with communities in Amazonas and Mato Grosso, Brazil

facts.text: Munduruku of the upper Tapajós created the Pusuru Indigenous Association in 1991 as a formal way to organize their communities.
The Munduruku language belongs to its own Munduruku family within the Tupi language stock.

nations.name: Waorani
nations.lands: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

facts.text: Waorani territory includes 32 communities in three Amazonian provinces of Ecuador: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo.
The legally recognized Waorani territory is governed by NAWE, the Waorani Nationality of Ecuador, regarded as the highest Waorani territorial authority.

nations.name: Huni Kuin
nations.lands: Rivers of Acre state in western Brazil, such as the Tarauacá, Jordão and Purus, and the Purus and Curanja rivers in Peru

facts.text: Huni kuin, the name the people use for themselves, means true people, or people with known customs.

source.title: Huni Kuin (Kaxinawá) - Povos Indígenas no Brasil

facts.text: MAHKU, the Huni Kuin Artists Movement founded in Acre in 2013, painted a large mural across the facade of the Central Pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale.

source.title: Biennale Arte 2024 | MAHKU (Movimento dos Artistas Huni Kuin)

nations.name: Tsimane'
nations.lands: Forests and savannas of the Beni department, Bolivia, mainly along the Maniquí and Apere rivers

facts.text: Tsimane' livelihoods center on small farms of plantains, rice, corn and sweet manioc, along with fishing, hunting and gathering.

source.title: Tsimane fieldsite in Bolivia
source.publisher: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield

facts.text: Almost all Tsimane' speak their own Tsimane' language as their main language.

source.title: Tsimane fieldsite in Bolivia
source.publisher: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield

nations.name: Asháninka
nations.lands: Central Peruvian Amazon in Junín, Ucayali, Pasco, Cusco, Huánuco and Ayacucho

facts.text: In 2017, 73,567 people in Peru said Ashaninka was the language they learned to speak as children.

source.title: Ashaninka | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Peru's 2017 national census, 55,493 people identified as part of the Asháninka people.

source.title: Ashaninka | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

nations.name: Wounaan
nations.lands: Darién and eastern Panama, including the Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands, and the San Juan River region of Colombia

facts.text: Wounaan forest technicians map illegal clearing with smartphone apps and GIS, and communities bring that evidence to the Wounaan National Congress.

source.title: Panama's Indigenous Groups Wage High-Tech Fight for Their Lands
source.publisher: Yale Environment 360, Yale School of the Environment

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 10,634 Wounaan people.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: K'iche'
nations.lands: Western highlands of Guatemala, including Quiché, Totonicapán, Quetzaltenango and Sololá

facts.text: In Totonicapán, the 48 Cantones is a K'iche' ancestral authority built from community governments, with representatives chosen each year in assembly.

source.title: Former Indigenous authorities of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán released in Guatemala after more than a year in pretrial detention

facts.text: The 48 Cantones' system of caring for forests and water has served as an example for communities all over Guatemala.

nations.name: Q'eqchi'
nations.lands: Alta Verapaz, Izabal and Petén in Guatemala, and the Toledo District of southern Belize

facts.text: Radio Chiquixji in Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, broadcasts for bilingual Q'eqchi' and Spanish speakers and for communities that speak only Q'eqchi'.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

facts.text: In southern Belize, 39 Q'eqchi' and Mopan Maya communities have rights to their customary lands, as Belize's highest appeals court affirmed in 2015.

source.title: Maya Leaders Alliance Advocates at United Nations Urging Respect for Rule of Law in Belize

nations.name: Cabécar
nations.lands: Indigenous territories in the Talamanca mountains and Chirripó area of Costa Rica, in Limón, Cartago and Puntarenas provinces

facts.text: Costa Rica's 2011 census found that 87.6 percent of people in the official Cabécar territories speak the Cabécar language.
Costa Rica's 2013 list of Indigenous territories includes Cabécar territories such as Alto Chirripó, Bajo Chirripó, Talamanca Cabécar, Ujarrás and Telire.

source.title: Anexo 6: Pueblos y territorios indígenas de Costa Rica (2013)

nations.name: Buglé
nations.lands: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and nearby areas of Bocas del Toro and Veraguas in western Panama

facts.text: Under Panama's 1997 comarca law, the comarca's General Congress is the highest body for the ethnic and cultural voice and decisions of the Ngäbe-Buglé people.

source.title: Ley 10 de 7 de marzo de 1997, por la cual se crea la Comarca Ngöbe-Buglé
source.publisher: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

facts.text: Panama's 2023 census counted 23,898 Buglé people; about 12,000 of them live in the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca, which they share with the Ngäbe.

source.title: Cuadro 20. Población indígena en la República, por sexo, según provincia, comarca indígena, grupo indígena al que pertenece y grupos de edad: Censo 2023
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama

nations.name: Naso Tjër Di
nations.lands: The Naso Tjër Di comarca along the Teribe River in Bocas del Toro, northwestern Panama, near the Costa Rican border

facts.text: The Naso are led by a king who lives in Sieyik, where Panama's president came in 2020 to sign the law creating their comarca.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

facts.text: In December 2020 Panama created the 1,600 square kilometer Naso Tjër Di comarca, the result of decades of Naso efforts to secure their land rights.

source.title: Indigenous community wins recognition of its land rights in Panama

nations.name: Mopan
nations.lands: The Toledo District of southern Belize and nearby Petén, Guatemala

facts.text: In 2022 a Free, Prior and Informed Consultation Protocol for the Maya of southern Belize was adopted, and in 2025 a working draft on protecting Maya customary land tenure followed.

source.title: Closing Remarks at the Final Monitoring Hearing in Maya Leaders v The Attorney General of Belize [2015] CCJ 15 (AJ)

facts.text: A 2015 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment obliges Belize's government to mark out and register Maya village lands in the south and guard them against outsiders.

source.title: Maya Q'eqchi and Mopan of Southern Belize Win Major Land Rights Victory in International Appeals Court (statement by the Maya Leaders Alliance)

nations.name: Miskitu
nations.lands: The Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and La Moskitia in northeastern Honduras, along the Wangki (Coco) River

facts.text: In 2021 the Yapti Tasba community radio network, linked to Miskitu organization YATAMA, reached 17 Indigenous territories and 154 communities, 95 percent of them Miskitu.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

facts.text: Nicaragua's Caribbean Coast autonomy law affirms that Indigenous communities there have the right to keep and develop their languages and to bilingual education.

source.title: Pueblo Miskitu, YATAMA, and Yapti Tasba Radios Advance Indigenous Rights on the North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua

nations.name: Garifuna
nations.lands: Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, plus large diaspora communities

facts.text: In 2024, Belize observed Garifuna Settlement Day on 19 November as one of its official public holidays.
Most Garifuna communities today are in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize, and the Garifuna language is part of the Arawakan family.

source.title: Language, dance and music of the Garifuna

nations.name: Kalinago
nations.lands: The Kalinago Territory on the northeast coast of Dominica, in the eastern Caribbean

facts.text: In July 2024, voters in the Kalinago Territory elected their Kalinago Chief; the winning candidate received about 58 percent of the votes counted.
The Kalinago Territory has its own local government: a Chief and six councillors elected by residents every five years, alongside representation in Dominica's parliament.

source.title: The Kalinago Territory
source.publisher: Division of Culture, Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica

nations.name: Mayangna
nations.lands: The Bosawás region and North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua, with related Tawahka communities in Honduras

facts.text: After the 2020 hurricanes, Mayangna communities in Bonanza rebuilt together: they repaired 15 roofs collectively and planted 50 plots of grains, beans, corn and cassava.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

facts.text: Nicaragua's Bosawás Biosphere Reserve, in the Mosquitia region, is ancestral territory of the Mayangna and Miskitu peoples, whose rights there are recognized.

source.title: Mayagna Communities Work to Achieve Food Sovereignty after Hurricanes Iota and Eta

nations.name: Lenca
nations.lands: Western and southwestern Honduras (Intibucá, Lempira, La Paz and nearby departments) and eastern El Salvador

facts.text: COPINH runs Lenca community radio stations that share news bulletins, podcasts, interviews and training with Lenca communities.

source.title: Las palabras haciendo eco en los caminos del pueblo Lenca: COPINH

facts.text: A community journalism program trained 24 Lenca women and 17 men as community correspondents, starting during the COVID-19 pandemic.

source.title: Indigenous, Garifuna, and Feminist Community Correspondents Push for a More Inclusive Democracy

nations.name: Xinka
nations.lands: Santa Rosa, Jutiapa and Jalapa departments in southeastern Guatemala

facts.text: In May 2024 the Parliament of the Xinka People hosted Guatemala's president in San Juan de Arana, Cuilapa, where they signed a 13-point work agenda.

source.title: Alegres le abrimos las puertas de nuestra casa, como usted nos ha abierto las puertas del Palacio, dice el pueblo xinca al presidente Arévalo

facts.text: In Santa Rosa, the Xinka People's Council (COPXIG), a local cooperative and the departmental education office work together to restore and teach the Xinka language.

source.title: Historia e Identidad del Pueblo Xinka
source.publisher: Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Dirección General de Investigación

nations.name: Ch'ol
nations.lands: Northern Chiapas, Mexico, including Tila, Tumbalá, Palenque, Sabanilla and Salto de Agua

facts.text: La Voz de la Selva, a Chiapas public radio station on air since 2000 in Santo Domingo, Ocosingo, broadcasts in Spanish, Tseltal, Ch'ol and Lacandón.

source.title: XHSDM-FM La Voz de la Selva : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Maize is at the heart of Ch'ol culture, and many festivals follow the farming year, from preparing the fields and sowing to the harvest.

source.title: Ch'oles : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Ikoots
nations.lands: The lagoons and coast of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Oaxaca, Mexico: San Mateo del Mar, San Dionisio del Mar and San Francisco del Mar

facts.text: Ikoots women weave huipiles, tablecloths and napkins with thread dyed using the secretion of a sea snail, while men make fishing nets.

source.title: Huaves : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: In San Mateo del Mar the year turns on three main celebrations: Candelaria in early February, Corpus Christi at midyear and San Mateo on September 19.

source.title: Huaves : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Ngiwa
nations.lands: Southern Puebla, Mexico, in the Tehuacán region, including Tlacotepec de Benito Juárez, San Marcos Tlacoyalco and Los Reyes Metzontla

facts.text: Among the Popoloca, the mayordomía organizes festivals, defends shared interests and is a key source of community cohesion and identity.

source.title: Popolocas : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: Popoloca communities each specialize in a craft, such as pottery, palm weaving, maguey and izote fiber rope, or cotton spinning and weaving.

source.title: Popolocas : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Popoluca
nations.lands: Southern Veracruz, Mexico, in the Isthmus region, including Soteapan and Sayula

facts.text: At the local level, Popoluca towns keep a compact character, organized by neighborhoods in Soteapan and by blocks in Sayula.

source.title: Popolucas : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

facts.text: Christmas and Easter are the main Popoluca celebrations, along with the traditional Danza de la Malinche.

source.title: Popolucas : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Tseltal
nations.lands: The Highlands, north and Selva regions of Chiapas, Mexico, including Tenejapa, Oxchuc, Cancuc and Ocosingo

facts.text: K'in Radio, a Chiapas state public station in Ocosingo, broadcasts in Spanish and Tseltal.

source.title: XEOCH-AM K'in Radio : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Tseltal ranks third among Mexico's Indigenous languages, spoken by 7.9% of the country's Indigenous language speakers in 2023.

source.title: Estadísticas a propósito del Día Internacional de los Pueblos Indígenas (9 de agosto), Comunicado de prensa núm. 472/24
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (INEGI)

nations.name: Yokot'an
nations.lands: Tabasco, Mexico: Nacajuca, Centla, Centro, Jonuta and Macuspana

facts.text: La Voz de los Chontales, an INPI radio station in Nacajuca, Tabasco, opened on February 28, 2020 to strengthen the Yokot'an language.

source.title: XHCPBS La voz de los Chontales (FM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Yokot'an people say the name of their language means the true language.

source.title: XHCPBS La voz de los Chontales (FM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

nations.name: P'urhépecha
nations.lands: Michoacán, Mexico: the Meseta P'urhépecha, Lake Pátzcuaro, the Ciénega de Zacapu and the Cañada de los Once Pueblos

facts.text: Every February 2, the INPI station La Voz de los P'urhépechas in Cherán launches a new program schedule to welcome the P'urhépecha New Year.

source.title: XEPUR La Voz de los Purépechas (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Each of the four P'urhépecha sub-regions has its own way of electing civil and communal authorities and Consejos Mayores, by custom and without political parties.

source.title: XEPUR La Voz de los Purépechas (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

nations.name: Hñähñu
nations.lands: The Valle del Mezquital in Hidalgo, Mexico

facts.text: La Voz del Pueblo Hñähñu, an INPI station in Cardonal, Hidalgo, has broadcast since 1999 in Hñähñu, Nahuatl and Spanish to spread and revitalize original languages.

source.title: XECARH La Voz del pueblo Hña hñú (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Otomí people of the Valle del Mezquital call themselves Hñähñu, often explained as those who speak the nasal language, or those who speak two languages.

source.title: Otomíes : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Hach Winik
nations.lands: The Lacandon Jungle of eastern Chiapas, Mexico

facts.text: La Voz de la Selva, a Chiapas public station in Santo Domingo, Ocosingo, includes Lacandón among its broadcast languages, along with Spanish, Tseltal and Ch'ol.

source.title: XHSDM-FM La Voz de la Selva : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Outside-driven change seems to have strongly affected Hach Winik culture, but it has also generated a strong sense of community and a new awareness of their environment.

source.title: Lacandones : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Tsotsil
nations.lands: The Highlands (Los Altos) of Chiapas, Mexico, including Chamula and Zinacantán

facts.text: La Voz de los Vientos, an INPI radio station in Copainalá, Chiapas, broadcasts in Zoque, Tsotsil and Spanish.

source.title: XECOPA La Voz de los Vientos (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Tsotsil women are renowned artisans: in Chamula they make wool chamarros, and in Zinacantán finely embroidered ponchos.

source.title: Tsotsiles : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Me'phaa
nations.lands: La Montaña and Costa Chica regions of Guerrero, Mexico, including Malinaltepec, Acatepec, Tlacoapa and Zapotitlán Tablas

facts.text: La Voz de la Montaña in Tlapa, on air since 1979, keeps at least 60 percent of its airtime in the region's original languages, including Me'phaa.

source.title: XEZV La Voz de la Montaña (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Me'phaa, also called Tlapaneco, is a language unique to the state of Guerrero.

source.title: XEZV La Voz de la Montaña (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

nations.name: Tojol-ab'al
nations.lands: Las Margaritas, Comitán and the Meseta Comiteca of Chiapas, Mexico, near the border with Guatemala

facts.text: Brisas de Montebello, a Chiapas public station in La Trinitaria, broadcasts in Spanish, Tojolabal, Kaqchikel and Q'anjob'al.

source.title: XHCTN-FM Brisas de Montebello : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: Tojol-ab'al communities call the INPI station XEVFS in Las Margaritas, Chiapas, La Xuxepil; its sound archive holds more than 6,500 recordings.

source.title: XEVFS La Voz de la Frontera Sur (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

nations.name: Dibaku
nations.lands: La Cañada region of northeastern Oaxaca, Mexico, including Cuicatlán, Concepción Pápalo and Santos Reyes Pápalo

facts.text: Since 1991, La Voz de la Chinantla has broadcast with bilingual staff in Chinantec, Mazatec and Cuicatec, recording music and oral tradition with communities.

source.title: XEOJN La Voz de la Chinantla (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

facts.text: The Cuicatec region lies in northeastern Oaxaca, in the area known as La Cañada, covering about 8,400 square kilometers across ten municipalities.

source.title: Cuicatecos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

nations.name: Ahtna
nations.lands: Copper River basin and the upper Susitna and Nenana river areas, Alaska, United States

facts.text: A comprehensive Ahtna dictionary was published in 1990, building on language documentation that began in 1973.

source.title: Languages - Ahtna
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: Ahtna is the Athabascan language of the Copper River and the upper Susitna and Nenana drainages, home to eight Ahtna communities.

source.title: Languages - Ahtna
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Cup'ik
nations.lands: Chevak and the nearby Bering Sea coast of southwest Alaska, United States

facts.text: In Chevak the people and their language are called Cup'ik, and on Nunivak Island the related form is Cup'ig, each used in place of the word Yup'ik.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

facts.text: Hooper Bay-Chevak is one of the five dialects of the Central Alaskan Yup'ik language.

source.title: Languages - Central Yup'ik
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Dena'ina
nations.lands: Cook Inlet region of Southcentral Alaska, including the Kenai Peninsula and the Anchorage area, United States

facts.text: The Kenaitze Indian Tribe states its vision as assuring that the Kahtnuht'ana Dena'ina thrive forever.
Dena'ina is the only Alaska Athabascan language spoken in a coastal setting, and the only one spoken on both sides of the Alaska Range.

source.title: Languages - Dena'ina
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Hän
nations.lands: Eagle, Alaska, United States, and Dawson, Yukon, Canada, along the upper Yukon River

facts.text: Hän is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
The Hän language is spoken at Eagle in Alaska and at Dawson in Yukon, and language centers on both sides of the border have documented it.

source.title: Languages - Hän
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Koyukon
nations.lands: Villages along the Koyukuk River and the middle Yukon River, Interior Alaska, United States

facts.text: Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons for Denaakk'e and nine other Doyon region languages; its first courses came out in summer 2019 and are free.
The language name Denaakk'e comes from denaa, meaning people, plus a suffix meaning like, so it literally means like us.

source.title: Languages - Koyukon
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Tlingit
nations.lands: Coastal Southeast Alaska from Yakutat south to Ketchikan, United States, with citizens living worldwide

facts.text: The Central Council of the Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska is the tribal government for more than 38,000 Tlingit and Haida citizens worldwide.

source.title: Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska
source.publisher: Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska

facts.text: Sealaska Heritage Institute says young people who learned Lingít and other Southeast Alaska languages, once nearly lost to oppression, now teach them with help from fluent Elders.

nations.name: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq
nations.lands: Kodiak Archipelago, Alaska Peninsula, outer Kenai Peninsula and Prince William Sound, Alaska, United States

facts.text: At the Alutiiq Museum, fluent speakers, learners and linguists work together to record Sugt'stun and teach it to a new generation of speakers.
Sugpiaq, the people's traditional name for themselves, joins suk, meaning person, with piaq, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Alutiiq / Sugpiaq
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: CHamoru
nations.lands: Guam (Guåhan) in the Mariana Islands, a United States territory

facts.text: Guam's Department of Chamorro Affairs works to preserve, develop and promote CHamoru heritage, with a division devoted to language and culture.

source.title: About Us
source.publisher: Department of Chamorro Affairs, Government of Guam

facts.text: Guam's Public Law 12-132 made both English and CHamoru official languages of the island.

source.title: Role of Education in the Preservation of Guam's Indigenous Language

nations.name: Iñupiat
nations.lands: Northwest and Arctic Alaska, from Norton Sound to the North Slope and the Canadian border, United States

facts.text: Iñupiaq is taught in colleges, communities, schools and online, and even in immersion classes for young children before kindergarten.
Iḷisaġvik College in Utqiaġvik was founded to teach from an Iñupiaq cultural foundation, and in 2006 it became the first and only federally recognized tribal college in Alaska.

nations.name: Samoans
nations.lands: Tutuila, Aunuʻu and the Manuʻa Islands of American Samoa, a United States territory in the Samoan Islands

facts.text: In American Samoa, land is held communally under the guidance of village chiefs, the matai, and the national park there sits on land leased from local villages.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

facts.text: Fa'asamoa, the Samoan way of life, took shape over many centuries and remains the base of Samoan identity and everyday living.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

nations.name: Upper Tanana
nations.lands: Northway, Tetlin and Tok in eastern Interior Alaska, United States, with a small community across the border in Canada

facts.text: Née'aaneegn', the Upper Tanana language, is one of ten Doyon region languages for which Doyon Languages Online is creating introductory online lessons.
The Upper Tanana people's own name for their language is Nee'aaneegn'.

source.title: Languages - Upper Tanana
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

nations.name: Kankuamo
nations.lands: South-eastern foothills of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta near Valledupar, Cesar, Colombia, centered on Atánquez

facts.text: The Kankuamo resguardo, about 24,212 hectares near Valledupar, was collectively titled to the people in 2003.

source.title: Kankuamos, guardianes del equilibrio del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: In 2022 UNESCO recognized the ancestral knowledge system shared by the Kankuamo, Arhuaco, Kogui and Wiwa as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

nations.name: Mapuche
nations.lands: South-central Chile, especially La Araucanía and Santiago, and Patagonian provinces of Argentina such as Neuquén and Río Negro

facts.text: Most Mapuche in Chile today live in cities, with the largest groups in La Araucanía region and in the capital, Santiago.
Mapudungun, the Mapuche language, is still the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Chile.

nations.name: Diaguita
nations.lands: Huasco and Choapa valleys of Chile's Norte Chico, and northwestern Argentina

facts.text: The first Diaguita community constituted under Chile's Indigenous Law, the Estancia Agrícola Diaguita de los Huascoaltinos, formed in 2006.
Many people who self-identify as Diaguita in Chile live in the upper Huasco River basin, in the municipality of Alto del Carmen.

nations.name: Kichwa Otavalo
nations.lands: Otavalo and nearby communities such as Peguche in Imbabura province, northern Ecuador

facts.text: Hampiriypacha, a Kichwa Otavalo association of seed guardians, works to protect knowledge that women have passed down for generations.

source.title: Meet our 2022 Keepers of the Earth Fund Grant Partners

facts.text: Yarina, a Kichwa Otavalo family band started in 1984, plays original Indigenous rhythms on traditional Andean instruments and works to keep Kichwa traditions alive.

nations.name: Kichwa Puruwá
nations.lands: Chimborazo province in the central highlands of Ecuador

facts.text: The Puruwá people include the communities of Cacha, Colta, Licto and Guamote in Chimborazo, each with its own local character.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

facts.text: Ecuador's 2010 census counted 136,141 Kichwa Puruwá people, about 18.5 percent of the whole Kichwa nationality.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

nations.name: Nasa
nations.lands: Cauca department, especially Tierradentro and northern Cauca, with communities in Huila, Valle del Cauca, Tolima and Putumayo, Colombia

facts.text: The Nasa language is Nasa Yuwe. In Colombia's 2005 census, 41.9 percent of Nasa people reported speaking it.

source.title: Nasa (Paez), la gente del agua
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Aymara
nations.lands: The altiplano around Lake Titicaca and nearby valleys and cities of Bolivia and Peru, and the far north of Chile

facts.text: Aymara is a vital language in Peru, where the 2017 census counted 450,010 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

source.title: Aimara | BDPI
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios

facts.text: In Bolivia's 2024 census, more than one million people self-identified as Aymara, and more than one million as Quechua.

source.title: INE presenta resultados del Censo 2024 que muestran la transformación demográfica y avances sociales en Bolivia
source.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Estadística de Bolivia

nations.name: Wiwa
nations.lands: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Cesar and Magdalena, Colombia

facts.text: Through education policies the Wiwa established an alphabet for Damana, and they are working to have it taught alongside Spanish in schools.

source.title: Wiwa: la gente que da origen al calor
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

facts.text: Wiwa mochilas include the duadu, woven from pure cotton for personal belongings, and the suzu, made of fique fiber with colorful designs.

source.title: Wiwa: la gente que da origen al calor
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Kichwa Kañari
nations.lands: Cañar and Azuay provinces in the southern highlands of Ecuador

facts.text: In Cañar parish, the province's largest Indigenous organizational network brings together 15 communities and 5 cooperatives.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

facts.text: The Kañari keep a vigorous ethnic identity and a very strong organizational system, in which cooperatives and many kinds of organizations are very active.

source.title: Guía Nacional de Nutrición de las Nacionalidades y Pueblos Indígenas, Afroecuatoriano y Montubio
source.publisher: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador

nations.name: Misak
nations.lands: Resguardos of Guambía and Quisgó in Silvia, Cauca, and nearby municipalities of southwestern Colombia

facts.text: Misak traditional dress, including the man's blue wrap called lusi pal, stands as a lasting symbol of resistance and of how the Misak present themselves.

source.title: Misak (Guambianos), la gente del agua, del conocimiento y de los sueños
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

nations.name: Kichwa Kayambi
nations.lands: Around Cayambe in Pichincha province and neighboring areas of Imbabura, northern Ecuador

facts.text: In 2022 Kayambi water boards, communes and community organizations met with a national legislator to discuss issues including a new water law.

source.title: Asamblea ampliada y mesa de trabajo con el Pueblo Kayambi

facts.text: The Confederación del Pueblo Kayambi holds a General Assembly where its communities and organizations bring their proposals and demands.

source.title: Asamblea General con el Pueblo Kayambi

nations.name: Mansi
nations.lands: Ob and Irtysh basin in western Siberia, mainly Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug (Yugra), with small groups in Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Okrug and Sverdlovsk Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Luima Seripos, a newspaper in the Mansi language, first came out on 11 February 1989 and is still produced today in a joint newsroom with the Khanty paper.

source.title: Историческая справка
source.publisher: Khanty Mansi Mir (joint editorial office of the Khanty Yasang and Luima Seripos newspapers)

facts.text: Mansi rapper Yevgeny Anyamov, known as Bizzo, records his songs in Mansi and opened his own studio in his hometown of Ivdel to share his people's culture with youth.

nations.name: Nivkh
nations.lands: Lower Amur River in Khabarovsk Krai and Sakhalin Island, Russia

facts.text: The Nivkh speak a language isolate, probably one of the oldest languages of Eurasia. Its links to other languages have not been established.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Nivkh life was built on fishing and hunting, including sea mammals taken with spears or with nets woven from leather straps.

source.title: Нивхи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Luoravetlan
nations.lands: Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, northern Kamchatka Krai and the Nizhnekolymsky District of Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: Researchers at Russia's Kunstkamera museum published a 2018 study on the mobile dwellings of Chukchi reindeer herders, covering both traditions and innovations.

source.title: Arctic Research Center
source.publisher: Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera), Russian Academy of Sciences

facts.text: Carving bone and walrus ivory and embroidering with reindeer hair are long-standing Chukchi arts, practised alongside reindeer herding and hunting.

source.title: Чукчи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Even
nations.lands: Northeastern Siberia: Sakha (Yakutia), Magadan Oblast, Kamchatka, Chukotka and Khabarovsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: The Even language belongs to the Tungusic (Manchu-Tungus) branch and is close to Evenki. Even self-names include Even (local) and Orochel (reindeer people).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: The 2002 census counted 11,657 Even living in the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia).

source.title: Эвены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Itelmen
nations.lands: Tigilsky District on the west coast of Kamchatka Krai, with smaller groups in Chukotka and Magadan Oblast, Russia

facts.text: Western Itelmen is the Itelmen language that has been kept to the present day.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Fishing, above all for salmon, is the traditional Itelmen livelihood on Kamchatka.

source.title: Ительмены
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Ket
nations.lands: Yenisei River basin, mainly Turukhansky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia

facts.text: A Cyrillic writing system that Ket speakers actually use came into being in the late 1980s.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Ket is the only living language of the Yeniseian language family.

source.title: Кеты
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Inughuit
nations.lands: Avanersuaq (the Thule region) in northwest Greenland, centred on the town of Qaanaaq

facts.text: Hunting is still a significant part of the livelihood of several families in Qaanaaq, Greenland's youngest and northernmost town.
The Inughuit have their own language, or dialect, and a hunting culture that is distinctive in several ways.

nations.name: Yupik
nations.lands: Settlements on the eastern coast of the Chukchi Peninsula, Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, Russia, across the Bering Strait from Alaska

facts.text: Inuit from Chukotka became part of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 1992, a goal that was in ICC's vision from the very beginning.
Yupik hunters are regarded as originators of traditional whaling in the region, hunting walrus, seal and whale with harpoons.

source.title: Эскимосы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Evenki
nations.lands: Siberian taiga from the Ob River to the Sea of Okhotsk, with the largest group in Sakha (Yakutia), also Krasnoyarsk and Khabarovsk krais, Buryatia, Amur, Irkutsk and Zabaykalsky regions of Russia, and in China and Mongolia

facts.text: Evenki communities live across Russia, with the largest in Sakha (Yakutia), and Evenki also live in China and Mongolia.

source.title: Эвенки
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Evenki homelands span a huge part of the Siberian taiga, from the Ob River in the west to the Sea of Okhotsk in the east.

source.title: The Evenks
source.publisher: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)

nations.name: Dolgan
nations.lands: Taimyr Peninsula in Krasnoyarsk Krai (Taimyr Dolgan-Nenets District) and the Anabar District and city of Yakutsk in Sakha (Yakutia), Russia

facts.text: During an August 2026 folk culture expedition to Khatanga, the Dolgan dried-fish dish kerdiileek was added to the list of Taimyr's intangible cultural heritage.

source.title: Долганская юкола «кэрдиилээк» признана объектом нематериального наследия Таймыра
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

facts.text: Dolgan is a Turkic language, close to Sakha (Yakut), from which it separated through isolated development.

source.title: Долганы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

nations.name: Wajãpi
nations.lands: Wajãpi Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and the middle and upper Oyapock River in French Guiana

facts.text: In 1994 the Wajãpi began demarcating their own Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and founded the Council of Wajãpi Villages, known as Apina.

source.title: Wajãpi
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In French Guiana the Wayãpi live along the middle and upper Oyapock River.

nations.name: Wayana
nations.lands: Upper Maroni River and its tributaries in French Guiana, the Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers in Suriname, and the East Paru River in Pará, Brazil

facts.text: France recognizes Wayana as one of six Amerindian languages of French Guiana with the status of a language of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

facts.text: Among younger people on Brazil's East Paru River, the Wayana language has gained great prestige.

source.title: Wayana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Uwottüja
nations.lands: The Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers and the middle Orinoco, Amazonas state, Venezuela

facts.text: In 2020 Uwottüja communities of the Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers met at Pendare and declared themselves guardians of their territory.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

facts.text: The Uwottüja held their first congress as a people in 1984, uniting around the defense of their ancestral lands 'like one churuata, with one voice'.

source.title: Pronunciamiento del Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja de los habitantes de los cuatro ríos Autana, Cuao, Sipapo, Guayapo y el sector Orinoco Medio
source.publisher: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela

nations.name: Ye'kwana
nations.lands: Amazonas and Bolívar states in southern Venezuela, and the Auaris and Uraricoera rivers of Roraima, Brazil

facts.text: The name Ye'kwana, which the people use for themselves, entered Venezuela's census in 1982 and has almost fully replaced the outside name Makiritare.

source.title: Censo Nacional de Población y Vivienda 2011: Empadronamiento de la Población Indígena

facts.text: Among themselves the Ye'kwana use So'to, meaning 'people', while Ye'kwana can be translated as 'canoe people'.

source.title: Ye'kwana
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

nations.name: Teko
nations.lands: Camopi on the Oyapock River and Cayodé on the upper Maroni, French Guiana

facts.text: France lists Teko, formerly called Émerillon, among French Guiana's six Amerindian languages recognized as languages of France.

source.title: Langues de France et langues régionales en Guyane: bilan au 7 décembre 2015
source.publisher: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane

facts.text: Teko and Wayãpi are the two Tupi-Guarani languages spoken in the Amazonian Park of French Guiana, where Wayana belongs to the Carib family.

nations.name: Pemón
nations.lands: Savannas of southeastern Venezuela, the Kamarang River area of Guyana, and Roraima state in Brazil

facts.text: Taurepang, Arekuna and Kamarakoto communities share the self-name Pemon, a word meaning 'people' or 'us'.

source.title: Taurepang
source.publisher: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil

facts.text: In Guyana, Arekuna communities live on the banks of the Kamarang River.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Akawaio
nations.lands: Upper Mazaruni area and nearby river valleys of western Guyana, with Akawaio also counted in Venezuela's census

facts.text: Akawaio is one of the nine Indigenous languages covered by Guyana's language revival programme, which the government moved to restart in 2021.

source.title: Gov't to resume Amerindian language revival project
source.publisher: Department of Public Information, Government of Guyana

facts.text: Akawaio communities live in Guyana's Upper Mazaruni area and along the Barama, Upper Pomeroon, Wenamu and Upper Cuyuni rivers.

source.title: Indigenous Nations
source.publisher: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana

nations.name: Barí
nations.lands: Serranía de los Motilones and the Catatumbo and Oro river basins in Norte de Santander, Colombia, and Zulia state, Venezuela

facts.text: The Barí language, of the Chibcha family, is being passed on to new generations and has speakers of all ages.
Barí live in the foothills of Colombia's Serranía de los Motilones along the Catatumbo and Oro rivers, with settlements also in Zulia state, Venezuela.
